turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Phelps? Come through. Doctor's running late, so I'll do your blood pressure while you wait. Been a long morning, hasn't it.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Since twenty past. And I only came for this knee, not a full going-over. It's been a pain on the clutch.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): We'll get there. Sleeve up on this side, there's a plaster on the other arm.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Blood test last week. No idea if anyone's even looked at it. Don't blow that cuff up hard, it leaves a mark.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): I'll go steady. Feet on the floor, and don't chat for a second.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Right. One hundred and seventy-eight over one hundred and two. That's up. I'll take it again in a minute.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): White coat. It does this every single time I'm in here. The chemist wasn't bothered.
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): What figure did the chemist give you?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): One thirty over eighty. Something like that. Last Tuesday, or maybe the week before, I binned the slip.
[SEG0010] person_1 (NURSE): Okay. Are you on any tablets for blood pressure?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No. And don't let him start me on any today, I've got a late shift. I came about the knee.
[SEG0012] person_1 (NURSE): Not my call. Your list says atorvastatin, forty milligrams at night.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): It's twenty. They cut it. Forty gave me aching legs, legs are fine now. That screen's always behind.
[SEG0014] person_1 (NURSE): I won't alter it, I'll just tell him. Same arm again, sit quiet.
[SEG0015] person_1 (NURSE): Second one, one hundred and sixty-six over ninety-eight. Dropped a bit, still high for us.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the chair and the wait. I'm not walking round at one seventy-eight, whatever that machine thinks.
[SEG0017] person_1 (NURSE): Pulse is eighty-eight, regular. Oh, your wife grabbed me in the corridor. She says the knee's been bad since before Christmas.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): She wasn't asked. Two weeks. There was a niggle, fine, but not since Christmas. She talks for me and she gets it wrong.
[SEG0019] person_1 (NURSE): She also said you've been dizzy in the mornings.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I have not been dizzy. I said I was tired. Tell her to wait in the car.
[SEG0021] person_1 (NURSE): Alright. He's free. Mind the step on the way in.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, password again. Nearly there. Mr Phelps, what are we seeing you for?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): The right knee. I have said it twice already.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right knee, sorry, say it once more, I was on the login. How long's it been sore?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, if you mean properly sore. Bit of a grumble before that. Didn't stop me driving.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nurse has written your wife thinks it started before Christmas. I'm just asking.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Write two weeks. She's not the one on the pedal all day.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll record that you say a fortnight and she says longer, so it sits somewhere between the two and you don't agree. Which part of the knee?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Inside. The medial bit. Clutch, stairs, and if I sit in the van it seizes when I get out.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any swelling, or locking, or has it given way?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. It doesn't lock. It hasn't given way. It is stiff in the morning, that's the other thing.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stiffness for how long?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten minutes. Well, maybe twenty. Then I can get on, till I'm driving again.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): And pain relief, what are you using?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Two of the five-hundred ones, so a gram, when it's playing up. Not every day.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any ibuprofen, naproxen, that sort of thing?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): A couple of ibuprofen from the cupboard last week. Burnt my stomach, so I stopped. That's settled. I'm not taking them again.

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Leave them off, yes, particularly with the pressure. I've got one seventy-eight over one oh two, then one sixty-six over ninety-eight. Can you say those again, the font on here is ridiculous.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not repeating her numbers. Chemist was one thirty over eighty. It's white coat. I don't want tablets.

[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): No tablets today. We'll do home readings before anyone labels this. Might be white coat, might be that the pressure's actually up. I can't tell off two rushed clinic ones.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Finally. Thank you.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Um. Family history, while this letter tries to load. Anything relevant, or not really?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): My dad had a stroke. Only in passing, I'm not building a case. He was seventy-odd and he drank. That's not me. She was just banging on about blood pressure.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Father had a stroke, alright. And you're on the statin for the cholesterol, aren't you?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Cholesterol's been there for years, yeah, same old story. Dose is twenty though, not forty. Reduced in the summer. Don't ask me the date, I haven't got it.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): The twenty, every night?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. If the shift runs late I just forget. I'm not going to dress it up.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): So we don't know how many you actually swallow in a week. The letter won't open, I can't see who dropped it to twenty. Chest pain at all?
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. Tired, and unfit. Don't you write breathless.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't put that down as a yes. Headaches? Vision any different?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches. Eyes are the same as ever.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Salt? Do you put a lot on?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Never really thought about it.
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Too vague, we'll park that. Let me see the knee. It's logged me out. Again. Trousers up over it, if you would.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Third password. My shift is at two. I'm knackered and I've got a van to get to.

[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): No swelling to look at. Not warm. Tender right on the medial joint line. I can flex it to about ninety before you pull away. No crepitus that I can feel. Collaterals feel sound.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the bit, yeah. You don't need to poke it twice.
[SEG0060] person_3 (DOCTOR): I think this is probably early osteoarthritis, wear and tear. That's a working impression, not a definite label. It doesn't feel like a cartilage that's locked.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): So no scan, then.
[SEG0062] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not today. If it hasn't settled in six weeks we might do an x-ray. For now stay on the paracetamol, ice it after the long drives, and don't jam the knee under the wheel.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): I drive for a living. The clutch is the job.
[SEG0064] person_3 (DOCTOR): Move the seat back a notch, and get out and stretch on the longer runs. That's advice, not a row. A bit of walking on a day off beats sitting the whole time.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Day off. If one turns up.

[SEG0066] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pressure plan. We'll lend you a monitor. Morning and evening for seven days, sitting quietly, not just after a coffee, write them all down. The nurse will sort the machine on your way out.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): Homework. From a knee appointment. Brilliant.
[SEG0068] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back in a fortnight with the sheet, whether they're high or low. If the home ones are properly up we can talk about a tablet then. Nothing is being started today.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): I heard you. Chemist was one thirty over eighty, since it never got typed. Are we done?
[SEG0070] person_1 (NURSE): Got the monitor. Use the arm without the plaster, same arm each time, morning and night. Sheet comes back in two weeks with you.

spec.situation: Patient attends for something minor (a knee or a form) and the nurse finds high BP; BP read aloud twice with different numbers; patient says it is white coat; family history of stroke said in passing; no tablets started today, home monitoring arranged.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
